bloecke.md:
## The money market and the overnight rate

The [[Money market|money market]] is the market for loans with a term of up to one year, usually less than a week and often just a single night. Trading takes place between banks, central banks, governments, insurers and funds, in amounts that are out of the question for private investors. Nevertheless, this market determines how much interest arrives in your instant-access savings account at the end of the month.

The reference rate for this is the [[€STR]] (euro short-term rate). The ECB calculates it every business day from the unsecured overnight loans that banks have taken out. It is therefore an average of transactions actually settled, whereas the old Libor was a survey figure. For the business day 17 September 2026 it was 2.440%, calculated from 885 transactions by 47 reporting banks totalling €66.6 billion.

The €STR closely tracks monetary policy. It is consistently a few basis points below the ECB deposit facility rate, so since 16 September 2026 just under 2.50%. The reason is that no bank lends money overnight at a lower rate than it receives for a deposit with the central bank. Lenders without access to the deposit facility (money market funds, foreign central banks, large companies), by contrast, have to offer their money slightly below that rate. Every ECB interest rate change shifts the €STR from the day on which the new deposit facility rate applies, usually from the Wednesday after the meeting. Interest rates on instant-access savings accounts follow with a delay of weeks and rarely in full.

bloecke.md:
## Four ways to invest short-term money

Private investors have four ways of investing money in this market. They differ less in the interest rate than in legal form, availability and protection.

With an **instant-access savings account**, the money is held as a deposit with a bank. It is available every day and earns a variable rate. The interest rate only applies until further notice, because the bank may change it at any time.

With a **fixed-term deposit**, the money is invested for a fixed period, and the interest rate is locked in for that time. Early termination is usually not provided for in the terms or incurs penalty interest (Vorschusszinsen). If interest rates rise, you remain tied to the old rate; if they fall, that rate is secured. The fixed rate works in both directions.

The third option is **money market funds and money market ETFs**. They hold short-dated securities or track the €STR via a swap. Legally, their fund assets are kept separate from the assets of the management company, and the units are not deposits. If the fund company or the depositary goes bust, investors' assets remain unaffected. In return, there is no deposit protection and no promised interest rate.

The fourth option is **short-dated government securities** bought through a securities account. The German federal government issues [[Bubill (German Treasury bill)|Bubills]] with maturities of up to twelve months as discounted securities without a coupon, as well as Federal Treasury notes (Schätze) with a two-year maturity. If you hold such a security until maturity, the result is already fixed on the day you buy it; if you sell earlier, you bear the price risk.

bloecke.md: One example of the third option is the largest euro money market ETF (Xtrackers II EUR Overnight Rate Swap, LU0290358497). It manages around €23.2 billion (as of October 2026), costs 0.10% a year and tracks the Solactive €STR +8.5 Daily index. The premium of 8.5 basis points stems from the switch from the old EONIA to the €STR. Its performance shows how closely cash depends on monetary policy. The fund returned plus 2.10% over one year, plus 8.77% over three years (2.8% a year) and plus 11.21% over five years (2.1% a year). In the years with a negative deposit facility rate, the same fund slowly lost value. A money market ETF therefore offers no guarantee and delivers the market's overnight rate, whether interest rates are rising or falling. With the swap-based version there is also a collateralised counterparty risk; physically replicating money market funds instead hold Treasury bills and certificates of deposit.

An instant-access savings account at 2.40% earns €240 in interest in one year. The bank withholds 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) including solidarity surcharge, that is €63.30, leaving €176.70. An exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) prevents the deduction as long as the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 is sufficient.

With the money market ETF at 2.43%, the unit value rises by €243; nothing is distributed. In January, the advance lump sum is taxed: base return = €10,000 × 3.20% (2026 base interest rate, Basiszins) × 0.7 = €224. This amount is capped at the actual increase in value of €243; it therefore stays at €224, with tax of €59.08. Money market funds receive no partial exemption (Teilfreistellung). Tax on the rest of the increase in value is levied later, on sale.

After tax, the two routes are only a few euros apart. For the decision, availability and protection therefore matter more than tax.

## Scope and limits of [[Deposit protection|deposit protection]]

By law, €100,000 per customer per bank is protected, and for a joint account this applies to each holder, so up to €200,000. Compensation is paid out within seven working days. After certain life events (sale of an owner-occupied property, inheritance, severance pay, divorce, insurance payout), up to €500,000 is covered for six months.

The following restrictions apply to this protection:

- The limit applies to all of a customer's accounts at one bank combined. Three accounts at the same bank therefore share one limit, and several brand names often belong to a single banking licence.
- Only deposits are protected. Certificates and bearer bonds issued by a bank are debt securities; if the bank becomes insolvent, the investor only has a claim in the insolvency proceedings. Securities in a securities account do not need this protection because they belong to the customer.
- Deposit platforms arrange deposits with German banks and with banks elsewhere in the EU. With a foreign bank, the deposit protection scheme of its home country is responsible, and German flat-rate withholding tax is usually not withheld. The income must then be declared on the capital income schedule of the tax return (Anlage KAP), and an exemption order has no effect.
- The voluntary additional protection is being reduced. The deposit protection fund of the private banks currently covers up to €3 million per private individual; in 2023 it was still €5 million, and from 2030 the limit is to be €1 million.

On 3 March 2021, BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) imposed a moratorium on the Bremen-based Greensill Bank; on 16 March, insolvency and a compensation event were declared. By 5 April, around €2.7 billion had been paid out to more than 20,500 depositors, against customer deposits of more than €3 billion. Private customers got their money back. Around 50 local authorities and institutional investors, by contrast, received no compensation because they were excluded from protection. The town of Monheim had deposited €38 million with the bank. Deposit protection therefore protects private households, but not every depositor.

bloecke.md:
In September 2026, top offers were 4.00% to 4.25%. They applied to new customers, for three to six months and often only to newly deposited money up to a maximum amount. After that, the rate falls to the rate for existing customers, which is guided by the deposit facility rate and rarely reaches it.

Illustrative calculation for €20,000 over twelve months: 4.25% in the first half-year brings in €425. If the rate then falls to an assumed 1.75%, a further €175 is added, €600 in total or an effective 3.0%. A permanent offer at 2.60% brings in €520. The advantage is €80 gross and just under €59 after flat-rate withholding tax. This requires identity verification, another account and a date in the calendar on which the money has to be moved. A comparison that leaves out the fallback phase overstates the advantage of the teaser offer.

bloecke.md:
## Benefits and costs of cash

Howard Marks describes liquidity as patient opportunism. Investors who hold cash can act when an opportunity arises without having to sell something first. The value of this option rises when prices fall, that is, in phases when other investors are forced to sell. It is paid for with the return forgone compared with long-term investments. Cash itself is currently losing purchasing power after tax and inflation, 1.5% a year in the waterfall above, so around €1,500 on €100,000.

Over long periods, cash performs considerably worse than equities. Dimson, Marsh and Staunton measure a real return of 0.5% a year for the US money market from 1900 to 2025. One dollar grew to $69 in nominal terms and $1.80 in real terms, a gain in purchasing power of 80% in 126 years. Invested in equities, the dollar grew to 3,296 times its value in real terms. Since 1928, the US equity premium over the money market has been 6.65 percentage points a year.

For money that stays invested for a long time, cash is therefore the worst investment, and for money that will be needed soon, the only sensible one. Moreover, the option to buy when prices fall only has value if it is used. Investors who have been waiting for years for the right moment to get in bear the costs year after year without ever benefiting.

The interest on cash compensates for the loss of purchasing power, usually not in full, and is thus not a return. Whether money should be held as cash therefore depends on whether its purpose requires safety; the level of interest plays no role in this.

- Match the term to the purpose. Money that may be needed at any time belongs in an instant-access savings account or a money market fund, not in a two-year fixed-term deposit.
- Spread amounts over €100,000 across several banks rather than several accounts at the same bank, and check whether two brands belong to the same banking licence.
- Set up the exemption order where the income arises; it has no effect at foreign banks.
- Note promotional rates with their end date and include the fallback rate in the comparison.
- Before buying a money market ETF, check the bid-ask spread. With an annual return of just over 2%, a spread of 0.05% corresponds to just over a week's interest.

mitnehmen: The €STR is the interest rate for overnight money (2.440% on 17 September 2026), is systematically a few basis points below the ECB deposit facility rate of 2.50% and serves as the benchmark for all cash offers.

Instant-access savings, fixed-term deposits, money market funds and short-dated federal securities differ above all in legal form and protection; only instant-access savings and fixed-term deposits are deposits with statutory protection.

By law, €100,000 per customer per bank is protected (for a joint account, per holder), and after certain life events up to €500,000 for six months; the voluntary additional protection of the private banks falls to €1 million from 2030.
Promotional rates apply to new customers and only for a few months; the only comparable figure is the blended rate across the teaser and fallback phases.

With an overnight rate of 2.44%, 26.375% tax and 3.3% inflation, the real return on cash is around minus 1.5% a year; this loss of purchasing power is inherent in the system and is accepted in return for availability.

begriffe.text: The euro short-term rate is the reference rate of the euro money market. The ECB calculates it daily from completed unsecured overnight loans taken out by banks. On 17 September 2026 it was 2.440%.

Market for loans and deposits with maturities of up to one year. Participants are banks, central banks, governments, companies and funds. Private investors can only access it through deposits, funds or short-dated government securities.

Statutory protection of bank balances up to €100,000 per customer per bank, with payout within seven working days. After certain life events, up to €500,000 is protected for six months. Securities and debt securities issued by the bank are not covered.

Non-interest-bearing Treasury discount paper issued by the German federal government with a maturity of up to twelve months. It is issued below face value and repaid at 100%; the difference is the return.

Fund that holds short-dated interest-bearing securities or tracks the overnight rate via a swap. Its assets are kept separate from those of the management company and are therefore protected against its insolvency. However, it has no deposit protection and no promised interest rate.
